title: Why Employees Resist AI and How Companies Can Win Them Over n-win-them-over
author: Michael Blanding
summary: Blanding reports on work by Das Narayandas and Shunyuan Zhang arguing that AI adoption stalls for reasons of identity rather than capability. Their term for the category is self-disruptive technology: tools that improve performance while making the people who use them feel less expert and less visible. Against explanations that blame organisational readiness or institutional pressure, they locate the failure at the level of the individual role, and identify three specific threats. Role compression leaves employees with less to do and lower-status duties, control shift moves the judgement that made a role feel like one's own into the system, and span erosion leaves managers with titles but no kingdom. Faced with these, the authors say most people choose neither refusal nor real adoption but symbolic adoption, complying visibly while quietly undermining the tool. The prescription is a bundle of five identity-compatible advantages, rechartering roles in specific rather than vague terms, building decision guardrails, creating analytical overlays that make user expertise more visible, committing to redeployment pathways, and lending executive sponsorship so the redesigned role does not read as a quiet demotion.
points: Narayandas and Zhang define self-disruptive technologies as tools that raise performance while lowering the user's sense of expertise and visibility.
They name three mechanisms, role compression, control shift and span erosion, that turn a productivity gain into an identity threat.
Symbolic adoption is presented as the most common response, with employees complying visibly while undermining the tool quietly.
The five identity-compatible advantages are meant to be used together, since rechartering a role without a retraining pathway will not hold.
The researchers insist the fix is a redesigned value proposition rather than reassurance, specifying which forms of judgement become more visible once routine work is automated.
quotes: Some technologies face resistance not because they don't work well, but because they could change the professional roles of the people who use them. Automation and AI are a sharp example: They can improve performance while making employees feel less expert or visible in their jobs.

Despite the promise of artificial intelligence to ease workloads, at least 30% of generative AI projects will be abandoned—often, the researchers argue, not because the tools fall short, but because they are quietly rejected by the very employees they were designed to help
They ignore a very important gap: the motivations of individuals resulting from a crisis they are facing around their own identity," he says.
As judgment and expertise are automated along with daily tasks, employees may find themselves with less to do overall, and the duties they do have may feel lower in status.
What thins out is the user's sense of authorship: The judgment that made the role feel like theirs now sits with the system, even though the title and the seat remain.
People don't want to get adversarial or be identified as the curmudgeon who refuses to do things, so they adopt the technology symbolically, giving the impression they are using it.
The point is not simply reassurance; it is to redesign the value proposition so users can see how adoption preserves or enhances the identity, expertise, influence, and future value of their role.
The machine doesn't need to be impressed or convinced or motivated, but the human needs to understand how they can benefit," says Narayandas.
